Aim and objectives

Aim. To interpret every graph and diagram that appears in Paper B quickly and accurately.

At the end of this workbook, you should be able to:

  1. Interpret forest, funnel and L'Abbé plots, including heterogeneity and publication bias.
  2. Interpret Kaplan-Meier curves, ROC curves and cost-effectiveness planes and acceptability curves.
  3. Interpret box plots, histograms, scatter plots and CONSORT and PRISMA flow diagrams.
  4. Identify the key number or conclusion each diagram supports in an exam question.
  5. Complete all 30 worked challenges, scoring at least 24 (80%), before you open the working.
  6. Turn all 50 flashcards and mark at least 40 as 'Got it' by the end of today's session.

Scores on a four-item gambling screen against a structured diagnostic interview in 120 attenders at a debt advice service
The table shows scores on a four-item gambling screen against a structured diagnostic interview in 120 attenders at a debt advice service. Which cut-off (score at or above) gives the best overall balance between sensitivity and specificity, as judged by the largest sum of sensitivity and specificity?
  1. 0
  2. 1
  3. 2
  4. 3
  5. 4
Show the working
Answer: C 2

Every cut-off has its own sensitivity and specificity. A simple way to compare them is to add the two; the cut-off with the largest sum (equivalently the largest Youden index, sensitivity + specificity minus 1) is the one nearest the top-left corner of a ROC plot and is usually quoted as the optimal threshold when both errors matter equally.

Cumulative counts give: at 1 or more, sensitivity 38/40 = 95% and specificity 44/80 = 55% (sum 150); at 2 or more, 32/40 = 80% and 68/80 = 85% (sum 165); at 3 or more, 20/40 = 50% and 80/80 = 100% (sum 150); at 4, 8/40 = 20% and 100% (sum 120). The cut-off of 2 wins.

The exam also likes the 'middle value' heuristic: when sensitivity and specificity move in opposite directions across the cut-offs, the balance point is usually central. Verify it with the arithmetic rather than trusting the heuristic.

Rule: The best balanced cut-off maximises sensitivity + specificity (Youden's index), the point nearest the top left of a ROC curve.
Trap: Choosing the cut-off with specificity 100% because it 'looks cleanest', ignoring the collapse in sensitivity.
StepWorkingResult
1Cut-off 0: 100% + 0%100
2Cut-off 1: 38/40 = 95% plus 44/80 = 55%150
3Cut-off 2: 32/40 = 80% plus 68/80 = 85%165 (largest)
4Cut-off 3: 20/40 = 50% plus 80/80 = 100%150
5Cut-off 4: 8/40 = 20% plus 100%120
Sum sensitivity and specificity at every cut-off: 2 or more wins with 165, equivalent to a Youden index of 0.65.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Challenge 2 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.10
Cumulative proportion of clinical high-risk participants who developed a first psychotic episode, by study
A systematic review of 24 studies (2180 participants) estimated the risk of transition to a first psychotic episode in people meeting clinical high-risk criteria. The pooled transition risk was 27% over a mean follow-up of 30 months. To show the time course, the four studies that reported time-to-event data are plotted in the figure. What is the median time to transition in the studies shown?
  1. 365 days
  2. 450 days
  3. 540 days
  4. 730 days
  5. Cannot be determined from the curves
Show the working
Answer: E Cannot be determined from the curves

Median time to event is the time at which half the cohort has had the event. On a conventional Kaplan-Meier curve it is where the curve falls to 0.50; on the cumulative version it is where the curve rises to 0.50. Either way, if the curve never crosses the halfway line during follow-up, the median is undefined and should be reported as not reached.

The four curves end at 0.33, 0.15, 0.40 and 0.25 at 730 days. The highest, Marchetti 2013, is still ten percentage points short of 50%. No median can be read for any study, and certainly not for the group as a whole.

The exam's temptation is the end of the axis. A curve stopping at 730 days tells you how long people were followed, not when half of them transitioned.

Rule: On a cumulative incidence plot the median is where the curve reaches 0.50; if it never does, the median is not reached.
Trap: Reading the last time point as the median.
StepWorkingResult
1Median = time when the curve reaches 0.50Look for the 50% line
2Final heights at 730 days: Okonkwo 0.33, Lindqvist 0.15, Marchetti 0.40, Petrov 0.25Highest is 0.40
30.40 is below 0.50No curve crosses the line
4730 days is the end of follow-up, not a medianMedian not reached in any study
The highest curve stops at 0.40, ten points short of the halfway line, so no median can be read.

Source: Bland JM, Altman DG (1998). Survival probabilities (the Kaplan-Meier method). BMJ, 317: 1572.

Challenge 3 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.22
AnalysisResponse: new drugResponse: comparatorDifference
Intention to treat (all randomised)50%40%10 points
Per protocol (adherent patients only)58%40%18 points
Response rates in a superiority trial analysed both ways (illustrative)
The table shows the response rates from a superiority trial analysed both ways. Compared with a per-protocol analysis, an intention-to-treat analysis of a superiority trial generally
  1. Overestimates the treatment effect
  2. Underestimates the treatment effect
  3. Gives the same estimate
  4. Increases the risk of a type I error
  5. Is unaffected by non-adherence
Show the working
Answer: B Underestimates the treatment effect

Because ITT includes patients who did not take the treatment, any true effect is watered down. That is acceptable in a superiority trial, where a bias towards no difference is the safe direction. In equivalence or non-inferiority trials the opposite applies, and per-protocol analysis is also required.

Rule: ITT is conservative for superiority; per-protocol is conservative for equivalence trials.
Trap: Assuming ITT is always the most conservative choice.
TermFormula or meaningThis item
Intention to treatEveryone analysed as randomised, adherent or notDifference diluted towards zero
Per protocolOnly patients who followed the protocolLarger difference, but randomisation balance lost
Superiority trialAims to show a differenceDilution is the safe direction, so ITT is primary
Non-inferiority trialAims to show no worse thanDilution flatters the new drug, so per protocol is also needed
Type I errorFalse positiveNot increased by ITT
Non-adherent patients pull the two arms together, so ITT underestimates the effect in a superiority trial.

Source: Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? BMJ, 319: 670-674.

Challenge 4 · 13.5 Inference, errors, power and confidence intervals · 3.2.17
Odds of suicidal ideation in psychiatric patients who smoke compared with non-smokers: OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.48 to 2.70, p < 0.0001
The figure shows that psychiatric patients who smoke have higher odds of suicidal ideation than non-smokers: OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.48 to 2.70, p < 0.0001. Which inference is valid?
  1. The confidence interval does not indicate the size of the effect
  2. The degree of bias can be estimated from the confidence interval
  3. There is a 5% chance that the OR of 2.00 is a chance finding
  4. The confidence interval includes the value of no effect
  5. The association is statistically significant at the 5% level because the interval excludes 1
Show the working
Answer: E The association is statistically significant at the 5% level because the interval excludes 1

An interval of 1.48 to 2.70 that excludes 1 is statistically significant and tells you the effect is plausibly between a 48% and a 170% increase in odds. The p value confirms the result would be very unlikely under the null. Neither statistic can detect systematic error, and a p value is not the probability that the finding is a fluke.

Rule: CI shows size and precision of the effect; it says nothing about bias.
Trap: Equating a significant p with a 5% chance of error, or expecting the interval to reveal bias.
The whole interval from 1.48 to 2.70 lies above 1, so the odds are raised by at least 48% and the result is significant at the 5% level

Source: Gardner MJ, Altman DG (1986). Confidence intervals rather than P values. BMJ, 292: 746-750.

Using the same figure, how was triangulation achieved in this study?

Show the working
Answer: D By seeking the views of both service users and care coordinators (data source triangulation)

Triangulation types: data source, method, investigator and theory. Here, service users and coordinators view the CTO from different positions, and comparing their accounts tests and enriches the findings.

Different groups' perspectives compared: data source triangulation. The slip to avoid is choosing the theoretical lens.

Scores on a four-item gambling screen against a structured diagnostic interview in 120 attenders at a debt advice service
The table shows scores on a four-item gambling screen against a structured diagnostic interview in 120 attenders at a debt advice service. Using a score of 4, rather than 3 or more, to define a positive screen will produce which of the following effects?
  1. A rise in both sensitivity and specificity
  2. A fall in sensitivity but a rise in specificity
  3. A fall in sensitivity with no change in specificity
  4. A fall in both sensitivity and positive predictive value
  5. A fall in sensitivity but a rise in positive predictive value
Show the working
Answer: C A fall in sensitivity with no change in specificity

Moving the cut-off up reclassifies people who scored exactly 3 from positive to negative. Any of them with the disorder become false negatives (sensitivity falls). Any of them without the disorder become true negatives (specificity rises). If nobody without the disorder scored 3, there is nothing for specificity to gain.

At 3 or more: sensitivity 20/40 = 50%, specificity 80/80 = 100%. At 4 only: sensitivity 8/40 = 20%, specificity still 80/80 = 100%. PPV is 100% at both. So the only thing that changes is that 12 more true cases are missed.

The exam expects the reflex 'raise cut-off, specificity up'. Check the table: once the false positive cell is empty, raising the bar only costs you cases.

Rule: Raising a cut-off lowers sensitivity; specificity only rises if there were false positives left to remove.
Trap: Reflexively answering that specificity rises without checking that it was already 100%.
StepWorkingResult
1At 3 or more: sensitivity = (12 + 8) / 4050%
2At 4 only: sensitivity = 8 / 4020%
3Specificity at 3 or more = 80 / 80 (no unaffected person scored 3 or 4)100%
4Specificity at 4 only = 80 / 80100%
5PPV at both: 20/20 and 8/8100%
Raising the bar from 3 to 4 reclassifies the 12 cases who scored exactly 3 as negative: sensitivity halves from 50% to 20% and specificity cannot move from 100%.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Four-item gambling screen (score 0 to 4) against a structured diagnostic interview in 500 attenders at a debt advice service
A four-item screening questionnaire for gambling disorder, scored from 0 to 4, is completed by 500 attenders at a debt advice service. Every attender is also assessed with a structured diagnostic interview as the reference standard. The table shows the number of attenders at each score with and without gambling disorder. A screen is positive when the score is at or above the chosen cut-off. Which cut-off gives the highest positive likelihood ratio?
  1. A score of 1 or more
  2. A score of 2 or more
  3. A score of 3 or more
  4. A score of 4
  5. A score of 0 or more
Show the working
Answer: D A score of 4

The positive likelihood ratio tells you how much a positive result shifts the odds of disease. It rewards a very low false positive rate: as a cut-off becomes stricter, the denominator (1 minus specificity) can fall towards zero much faster than the numerator (sensitivity), so the LR+ climbs. The highest LR+ is therefore usually found at the strictest cut-off, even though that cut-off misses most cases.

Work through each cut-off. Score 1 or more: 48/50 = 0.96 sensitivity; non-cases positive = 120/450, specificity 0.73; LR+ = 0.96/0.27 = 3.6. Score 2 or more: 0.80 and 400/450 = 0.89; LR+ = 0.80/0.11 = 7.2. Score 3 or more: 0.50 and 430/450 = 0.96; LR+ = 0.50/0.044 = 11.3. Score 4: 0.20 and 445/450 = 0.99; LR+ = 0.20/0.011 = 18. The cut-off of 4 wins.

The exam expects you to notice that 'highest LR+' is not the same as 'best cut-off'. A score of 4 is a very strong rule-in result, but as a screen it misses four in five cases; the clinically sensible threshold is chosen from the ROC shoulder and the purpose of the test.

Rule: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 minus specificity): the strictest cut-off usually has the highest LR+, because the false positive rate shrinks faster than sensitivity.
Trap: Picking the cut-off that looks best overall (the ROC shoulder) instead of calculating the LR+ for each.
StepWorkingResult
Score 1 or moresens 48/50 = 0.96; FPR 120/450 = 0.267LR+ = 0.96/0.267 = 3.6
Score 2 or moresens 40/50 = 0.80; FPR 50/450 = 0.111LR+ = 0.80/0.111 = 7.2
Score 3 or moresens 25/50 = 0.50; FPR 20/450 = 0.044LR+ = 0.50/0.044 = 11.3
Score 4sens 10/50 = 0.20; FPR 5/450 = 0.011LR+ = 0.20/0.011 = 18.0
Positive likelihood ratio at each cut-off of the gambling screen: the strictest cut-off, a score of 4, gives the highest LR+ of 18

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 2: predictive values. BMJ, 309: 102.

Challenge 8 · 13.4 Measures of treatment impact · 3.2.12.2
Depressive episodeNo episodeTotal
Heavy drinkers (n = 200)50150200
Non-drinkers (n = 200)20180200
Total70330400
Depressive episodes over ten years in a cohort of 400 adults
In a cohort study, 200 heavy drinkers and 200 non-drinkers are followed for ten years. The table shows the results: 50 of the heavy drinkers and 20 of the non-drinkers develop a depressive episode. If 20% of the adult population are heavy drinkers, the proportion of depression in the population attributable to heavy drinking, using this study's figures, is
  1. 3/100
  2. 15/100
  3. 20/100
  4. 30/100
  5. 1/5
Show the working
Answer: A 3/100

The attributable risk tells you the extra risk carried by an exposed person. To find the burden on the whole population you scale it by how many people are exposed: a large excess risk in a rare exposure may contribute less to the population than a small excess risk in a common one.

Attributable risk = 50/200 minus 20/200 = 0.15. With 20% exposed, population attributable risk = 0.15 x 0.20 = 0.03, or 3 per 100 of the population. Three in every hundred adults in the population develop depression over ten years because of heavy drinking.

The exam asks the attributable risk and the population attributable risk in consecutive questions on the same data; the second is always the first multiplied by the stated prevalence.

Rule: Population attributable risk = attributable risk x proportion of population exposed.
Trap: Reporting the attributable risk and forgetting the prevalence multiplier.
Per 100 adults: the 20 heavy drinkers have 5 depressive episodes (25%), of which 3 are the excess over the 10% background; those 3 per 100 are the population attributable risk, 0.15 x 0.20 = 0.03.

Source: Last JM (2001). A Dictionary of Epidemiology, 4th ed. Oxford University Press.

Challenge 9 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.8
A 12-item psychological distress questionnaire against a diagnostic interview in 600 primary care attenders; each labelled point is a cut-off score
A 12-item psychological distress questionnaire is compared against a diagnostic interview in 600 primary care attenders. Each labelled point on the plot corresponds to a different cut-off score for a positive screen. Which cut-off score offers the best combination of high sensitivity with acceptable specificity?
  1. Cut 7
  2. Cut 8
  3. Cut 9
  4. Cut 10
  5. Cut 11
Show the working
Answer: B Cut 8

Each point on a ROC curve is a cut-off, and moving along the curve trades sensitivity for specificity. The point that maximises sensitivity plus specificity, equivalently the one furthest from the diagonal line of no discrimination and closest to the top-left corner, is the usual choice when neither type of error is weighted more heavily. This is the maximum of the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity minus 1).

Reading the plot: cut 8 gives sensitivity 0.90 and false positive rate 0.20, a Youden index of 0.70. Cut 9 gives 0.72 and 0.12 (index 0.60); cut 7 gives 0.95 and 0.40 (index 0.55). Cut 8 is the shoulder: beyond it the curve flattens, so extra sensitivity costs a lot of specificity, and before it the curve is steep, so extra specificity costs a lot of sensitivity.

The exam may word this as 'best mixture of sensitivity and specificity' or 'optimal cut-off'. Look for the point where the curve turns from steep to flat. If the stem instead says the test is for ruling out, lean towards the more sensitive point; if for confirming, towards the more specific one.

Rule: The best overall cut-off is at the shoulder of the ROC curve, the point nearest the top-left corner (highest sensitivity plus specificity).
Trap: Choosing the cut-off with the highest sensitivity regardless of how many false positives it brings.
StepWorkingResult
Cut 110.30 + 0.98 minus 1Youden 0.28
Cut 100.55 + 0.94 minus 1Youden 0.49
Cut 90.72 + 0.88 minus 1Youden 0.60
Cut 80.90 + 0.80 minus 1Youden 0.70
Cut 70.95 + 0.60 minus 1Youden 0.55
Youden's index (sensitivity plus specificity minus 1) at each cut-off peaks at 0.70 for cut 8, the shoulder of the curve

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

A four-item screening questionnaire for gambling disorder, scored from 0 to 4, is completed by 500 attenders at a debt advice service. Every attender is also assessed with a structured diagnostic interview as the reference standard. The table shows the number of attenders at each score with and without gambling disorder. A screen is positive when the score is at or above the chosen cut-off. If the cut-off is raised from a score of 2 or more to a score of 3 or more, which of the following is most likely?
  1. Sensitivity falls and positive predictive value rises
  2. Sensitivity falls and specificity is unchanged
  3. Sensitivity rises and specificity rises
  4. Sensitivity is unchanged and specificity rises
  5. Sensitivity falls and positive predictive value falls
Show the working
Answer: A Sensitivity falls and positive predictive value rises

Moving the threshold up reclassifies everyone at the old threshold as negative. True cases at that score become false negatives (sensitivity falls, NPV falls slightly); non-cases at that score become true negatives (specificity rises). Because false positives shrink proportionally more than true positives, the fraction of positive results that are genuine, the PPV, rises.

In the table, going from 2 or more to 3 or more moves 15 cases and 30 non-cases out of the positive group. Sensitivity drops from 40/50 (0.80) to 25/50 (0.50). Specificity rises from 400/450 (0.89) to 430/450 (0.96). PPV rises from 40/90 (0.44) to 25/45 (0.56). Every arrow follows the rule.

The exam phrases this as 'if cut-off X is used instead of Y'. Decide whether the threshold moved up or down, then apply the four-arrow rule; distractors always pair one correct direction with one wrong one.

Rule: Raising the cut-off: sensitivity down, specificity up, PPV up, NPV down.
Trap: Assuming that specificity is fixed and only sensitivity moves when the threshold changes.
StepWorkingResult
Sensitivity40/50 at 2 or more; 25/50 at 3 or more0.80 falls to 0.50
Specificity400/450 at 2 or more; 430/450 at 3 or more0.89 rises to 0.96
PPV40/90 at 2 or more; 25/45 at 3 or more0.44 rises to 0.56
Who moved15 cases and 30 non-cases scoring exactly 2 become screen negativeFewer positives, a larger share of them genuine
Raising the cut-off from 2 to 3 drops sensitivity from 0.80 to 0.50 while specificity rises to 0.96 and PPV rises from 0.44 to 0.56

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Challenge 11 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.10
Time to first relapse after a first episode of psychosis: 300 patients randomised to an early intervention service or standard care
The Kaplan-Meier plot shows time to first relapse in 300 patients with first-episode psychosis randomised to an early intervention service or standard community care, followed for 36 months. How many patients in the standard care arm were still at risk of a first relapse at 18 months?
  1. 43
  2. 45
  3. 61
  4. 88
  5. 104
Show the working
Answer: C 61

The table printed under a survival curve lists the number of patients still under observation at each time point: those who have not yet had the event and have not been censored. It falls over time because of both events and censoring. It tells you how much information lies behind each part of the curve, which is why it matters more at the right-hand end.

Look along the standard care row to the 18-month column: 61 patients. Note that 61 of 150 is 41%, close to but not the same as the survival estimate of 0.43, because censored patients leave the count at risk without counting as events.

The exam likes to offer the survival proportion disguised as a count (43 here) and the other arm's figure. Read the row for the arm and the column for the time, and do not try to compute the number from the curve.

Rule: The numbers at risk table counts patients still being followed and event free at each time.
Trap: Confusing the survival proportion with the number at risk.
TermFormula or meaningThis item
Number at risk at 18 monthsPatients still under observation, not yet relapsed or censoredStandard care: 61 (read from the table): the answer
Survival proportion at 18 monthsEstimated share of the starting cohort still relapse-free0.43
Why they differCensored patients leave the at-risk count without counting as relapses61/150 = 41%, not 43%
Other arm at 18 monthsEarly intervention row104
Same arm at 24 monthsNext column along45
The at-risk table counts people still being watched; the curve estimates a proportion. Read the table for a count.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1998). Time to event (survival) data. BMJ, 317: 468-469.

Challenge 12 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.11
ItemValue

Outcome of an admitted cohort with a severe infection
Of 200 patients admitted with a severe infection, 30 die during admission, as the table shows. The figure 15% is the
  1. Crude death rate
  2. Case fatality rate
  3. Standardised mortality ratio
  4. Incidence rate
  5. Proportional mortality
Show the working
Answer: B Case fatality rate

Case fatality measures how lethal a condition is once you have it. It is a proportion, usually over a defined period such as the admission or 30 days.

Rule: Case fatality = deaths from the disease / cases of the disease.
Trap: Confusing with mortality rate, which divides by the whole population.
Case fatality = 30/200 = 15%: of every 20 admitted, 3 die

Source: Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Blackwell.

Challenge 13 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.11
ItemValue

Observed and expected deaths in a cohort of people with schizophrenia
A cohort of people with schizophrenia experiences 150 deaths over ten years. Applying age- and sex-specific death rates from the general population to the cohort gives an expected 60 deaths, as the table shows. The standardised mortality ratio is
  1. 0.4
  2. 2.5
  3. 40%
  4. 250 per 1,000
  5. 90
Show the working
Answer: B 2.5

The SMR is an indirectly standardised measure. An SMR of 2.5 means two-and-a-half times the mortality expected for a population of the same age and sex structure. Most studies of severe mental illness report SMRs between 2 and 3.

Rule: SMR = observed deaths / expected deaths. SMR 1 (or 100) = no excess.
Trap: Inverting the ratio.
150 observed against 60 expected: SMR = 150/60 = 2.5, with 90 excess deaths

Source: Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Blackwell.

Challenge 14 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.8
ROC curves for two bedside delirium screening tools against a reference psychiatric assessment in 420 older medical inpatients
The ROC curves compare two bedside delirium screening tools, the Ward Confusion Screen (WCS) and the Brief Attention Test (BAT), against a reference psychiatric assessment in 420 older medical inpatients. Labelled points show the sensitivity and false positive rate at each cut-off score. Which tool has the better overall discriminating ability, and why?
  1. The BAT, because its curve lies closer to the diagonal
  2. The WCS, because its curve lies closer to the top left corner and its area under the curve is larger (0.90 versus 0.76)
  3. The BAT, because it has fewer cut-off points
  4. They are equivalent, because both curves start at (0,0) and end at (1,1)
  5. The WCS, because its cut-off scores are higher
Show the working
Answer: B The WCS, because its curve lies closer to the top left corner and its area under the curve is larger (0.90 versus 0.76)

A ROC curve plots sensitivity against 1 minus specificity (the false positive rate) for every possible cut-off. A perfect test would go straight up the left edge to the top left corner (sensitivity 1, false positive rate 0). A useless test runs along the diagonal. The area under the curve summarises accuracy across all cut-offs: 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect, and roughly 0.8 or more is considered good.

The WCS reaches sensitivity 0.78 at a false positive rate of only 0.10 (cut 6), while the BAT needs a false positive rate of 0.38 to reach 0.76 (cut 3). The WCS curve lies above and to the left of the BAT curve at every point, and its AUC is 0.90 against 0.76. The WCS is the better discriminator at any cut-off you choose.

The exam shows two or three curves and asks which test is best or which AUC goes with which curve. If the curves cross, the answer depends on which part of the curve matters clinically; here they do not cross, so the answer is unambiguous.

Rule: The ROC curve nearer the top left corner, with the larger AUC, is the better test.
Trap: Choosing the curve nearer the diagonal.
Cut-offWCS sensitivityWCS false positive rateBAT sensitivityBAT false positive rate
Strictest0.52 (cut 8)0.040.38 (cut 5)0.08
0.78 (cut 6)0.100.60 (cut 4)0.20
0.92 (cut 4)0.220.76 (cut 3)0.38
Most lenient0.98 (cut 2)0.450.88 (cut 2)0.60
AUC0.900.76
At every cut-off the WCS buys more sensitivity for fewer false positives; its curve lies above the BAT's throughout and its AUC is 0.90 against 0.76.

Source: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

Challenge 15 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.10
Kaplan-Meier curves for time to relapse: steps are relapses, short vertical ticks are censored participants, the dashed line marks 50%
In the same figure, the small vertical ticks on the curves represent
  1. Relapses
  2. Deaths from other causes only
  3. Censored observations
  4. Confidence limits
  5. Time points at which the log-rank test was applied
Show the working
Answer: C Censored observations

A censored participant leaves the at-risk group at the time of the tick. The curve does not step down because no event occurred, but subsequent steps become larger because fewer people remain at risk.

Rule: Steps = events; ticks = censored.
Trap: Treating censored participants as events or discarding them.
The ticks on a Kaplan-Meier curve are these censored people: Chen and Ella leave early without relapsing and Amira and Farah are still well at 24 months; only Ben and Dev make steps

Source: Bewick V, Cheek L, Ball J (2004). Statistics review 12: survival analysis. Crit Care, 8: 389-394.

Challenge 16 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.8
ROC curve for the Worry Screening Scale against a structured clinical interview, with six candidate cut-off scores
A 20-item self-report worry scale was tested against a structured diagnostic interview for generalised anxiety disorder in 400 primary care attenders. The curve plots the performance of six candidate cut-off scores (a score at or above the cut-off counts as a positive screen). Which cut-off offers the best overall balance between sensitivity and specificity?
  1. Cut-off 3
  2. Cut-off 5
  3. Cut-off 7
  4. Cut-off 9
  5. Cut-off 11
Show the working
Answer: D Cut-off 9

Every cut-off trades sensitivity for specificity. The point that balances the two best is the one closest to the perfect test at the top left corner (sensitivity 1, false positive rate 0), which is the same as maximising Youden's index, sensitivity plus specificity minus 1. On most curves this is the visible 'knee' where the curve stops climbing steeply and starts flattening.

Working the numbers from the figure: cut-off 7 gives 0.86 + 0.70 = 1.56; cut-off 9 gives 0.80 + 0.88 = 1.68; cut-off 11 gives 0.58 + 0.95 = 1.53. Cut-off 9 wins comfortably, and it is also where the curve visibly turns. The distance to the corner tells the same story: about 0.23 for cut-off 9 against 0.33 for cut-off 7.

Remember that 'best balance' is a statistical answer. If the test is being used to screen, where missing a case is costly, you would deliberately slide down to a lower cut-off and accept more false positives.

Rule: The best-balanced cut-off is the point nearest the top left corner, where sensitivity plus specificity peaks.
Trap: Choosing the highest-sensitivity point rather than the one nearest the corner.
At cut-off 9 the scale catches 80 of 100 cases and clears 88 of 100 non-cases: sensitivity + specificity = 1.68, higher than cut-off 7 (1.56) or cut-off 11 (1.53).

Source: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

Challenge 17 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.11
All-cause SMR over five years in two treatment settings for anorexia nervosa
A registry study reports the five-year all-cause standardised mortality ratio in people with anorexia nervosa who received inpatient care as 310 (95% CI 248 to 372), and in those who received outpatient care only as 112 (95% CI 88 to 136), shown in the figure. Which interpretation is correct?
  1. Outpatient-only care is associated with significantly higher mortality than the general population of the same age and sex
  2. Mortality is significantly lower in the inpatient group than in the outpatient-only group
  3. Mortality is significantly higher in the inpatient group than in the outpatient-only group
  4. Neither group differs significantly from the general population
  5. Both groups have significantly higher mortality than the general population
Show the working
Answer: C Mortality is significantly higher in the inpatient group than in the outpatient-only group

An SMR of 100 means the study group has exactly the mortality expected from reference-population rates. The 95% confidence interval shows the precision: if it includes 100 the difference from the reference population could be chance; if it lies entirely above or below 100 the difference is statistically significant. To compare two SMRs with each other, look at whether their intervals overlap; clearly non-overlapping intervals indicate a significant difference (overlapping intervals are less conclusive).

The inpatient group's interval runs from 248 to 372 and sits well above 100, so its mortality is significantly higher than expected, roughly three times the general population. The outpatient-only group's interval (88 to 136) straddles 100, so its mortality is not demonstrably different from the general population. The two intervals do not come close to overlapping, so the inpatient group has significantly higher mortality than the outpatient-only group.

Note that this is an association, almost certainly reflecting illness severity determining the care setting, not evidence that admission causes death; the exam asks only what the statistics say.

Rule: SMR CI including 100 = not different from the reference population; non-overlapping CIs between groups = significant difference between them.
Trap: Concluding the outpatient-only group is significantly above the population because 112 is above 100, ignoring that the interval includes 100.
StepWorkingResult
1Inpatient SMR 310, CI 248 to 372: does the CI include 100?no: significantly above the general population
2Outpatient-only SMR 112, CI 88 to 136: does the CI include 100?yes: not demonstrably different
3Do the two intervals overlap? 248 to 372 versus 88 to 136no: a gap of 112 between them
4Conclusioninpatient mortality significantly higher than outpatient-only (keyed)
Working through the two intervals against 100 and against each other

Source: Gardner MJ, Altman DG (1986). Confidence intervals rather than P values. BMJ, 292: 746-750.

Challenge 18 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.24
Relapse at 12 months: family intervention versus treatment as usual, 7 randomised trials (events/total shown for family intervention then treatment as usual)
The forest plot summarises seven randomised trials of family intervention versus treatment as usual in schizophrenia, with relapse at 12 months as the outcome, reported as odds ratios. The authors used a random-effects model. Compared with a fixed-effect analysis of the same seven trials, which statement is correct?
  1. The random-effects model assumes all trials estimate a single common effect
  2. The random-effects model gives more equal weights across trials, so Castellano 2014 would carry even more weight under a fixed-effect model
  3. The random-effects confidence interval will be narrower than the fixed-effect interval
  4. A random-effects model should only be used when I2 exceeds 75%
  5. With Tau2 = 0.03 the two models cannot give different answers
Show the working
Answer: B The random-effects model gives more equal weights across trials, so Castellano 2014 would carry even more weight under a fixed-effect model

A fixed-effect model assumes every trial is estimating the same true effect and that differences are sampling error only; weights are 1 / within-study variance, so large trials dominate. A random-effects model assumes the true effects vary from trial to trial around an average, with between-study variance Tau2; weights become 1 / (within-study variance + Tau2). Adding the same Tau2 to every study evens out the weights and widens the pooled interval.

Here Tau2 = 0.04 and I2 = 31%. Under random effects Castellano 2014 carries 27.5%; under fixed effects it would carry about 36%, and Petrova 2007 would fall from 1.8% to about 1%. Because the trials broadly agree the pooled OR barely moves (0.58 random effects against 0.57 fixed effect), but the random-effects CI of 0.43 to 0.77 is wider than the fixed-effect interval of about 0.46 to 0.71.

The exam asks which model to choose and what changes: random effects when the trials plausibly differ in populations or delivery, which is nearly always the case for complex psychosocial interventions. Expect wider CI and more even weights; the estimate itself may or may not shift.

Rule: Fixed = one true effect, weights by precision alone; random = distribution of effects, more even weights, wider CI.
Trap: Thinking random effects narrows the interval or should only be used at very high I2.
Adding the same Tau2 to every study evens the weights: Castellano falls from about 36% under fixed effect to 27.5% under random effects while the small trials gain.

Source: Higgins JPT, Thompson SG, Deeks JJ, Altman DG (2003). Measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses. BMJ, 327: 557-560.

Challenge 19 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.26
Relapse at 12 months: family intervention versus treatment as usual, 7 randomised trials (events/total shown for family intervention then treatment as usual)
The forest plot summarises seven randomised trials of family intervention versus treatment as usual in schizophrenia, with relapse at 12 months as the outcome, reported as odds ratios. In a sensitivity analysis the authors re-ran the meta-analysis after removing Castellano 2014. Which result is most likely?
  1. The pooled odds ratio moves slightly towards 1 and its confidence interval widens, but it still excludes 1
  2. The pooled odds ratio becomes exactly the simple average of the six remaining point estimates
  3. The pooled odds ratio rises above 1, reversing the conclusion
  4. The confidence interval narrows because an influential study has been removed
  5. I2 rises sharply because the most precise study has been removed
Show the working
Answer: A The pooled odds ratio moves slightly towards 1 and its confidence interval widens, but it still excludes 1

A sensitivity analysis repeats the meta-analysis under a different decision: leaving out one study (often the largest, the lowest quality or the outlier), switching from random to fixed effects, or restricting to blinded trials. If the pooled estimate and its significance barely change, the conclusion is robust. If they change materially, the result depends on that decision and the review should say so.

Removing Castellano 2014 takes out 27.5% of the weight and the study with one of the lower odds ratios (0.47). The six remaining trials have ORs of 0.39, 0.38, 0.62, 0.89, 0.89 and 0.15 and a random-effects pool of about 0.62. With less information the interval widens, to about 0.44 to 0.88, but every remaining study points in the same direction so the interval still excludes 1 and the conclusion stands.

The exam phrases this as 'leave-one-out' or 'the result was robust to exclusion of'. Reason from the weights and the direction of the remaining studies rather than from the size of the removed study's effect alone.

Rule: Sensitivity analysis asks whether the conclusion survives when one study or assumption is changed.
Trap: Assuming that removing the biggest study must overturn the result, or that it narrows the interval.
Dropping Castellano 2014 (OR 0.47, 27.5% weight) nudges the pool from 0.58 to about 0.62 and widens the interval to about 0.44 to 0.88, still clear of 1.

Source: Higgins JPT, Thompson SG, Deeks JJ, Altman DG (2003). Measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses. BMJ, 327: 557-560.

Challenge 20 · 13.4 Measures of treatment impact · 3.2.12.2
New depressionNo depressionTotal
Bullied at work (n = 400)60340400
Not bullied (n = 2400)12022802400
Total18026202800
New-onset depression over five years by exposure to workplace bullying
A five-year cohort study of adults in a northern English city follows 400 people who experienced bullying at work and 2400 who did not. The table shows the results: new-onset depression occurs in 60 of the bullied group and 120 of the non-bullied group. Of the depression that arises among bullied workers, what proportion is attributable to the bullying?
  1. 0.10
  2. 0.33
  3. 0.67
  4. 0.03
  5. 3.0
Show the working
Answer: C 0.67

The attributable risk among the exposed is the incidence in the exposed minus the incidence in the unexposed: the extra risk an exposed person carries. Dividing that excess by the incidence in the exposed turns it into a fraction: the share of cases among exposed people that would not have happened without the exposure. Because the fraction is a ratio of risks, it can also be written in terms of the relative risk as (RR minus 1) / RR.

Incidence in the bullied = 60/400 = 0.15. Incidence in the non-bullied = 120/2400 = 0.05. Attributable risk = 0.10. Attributable fraction among the exposed = 0.10 / 0.15 = 0.67. The same answer comes from the relative risk: RR = 3, so (3 minus 1) / 3 = 0.67. Two thirds of the depression among bullied workers is attributable to the bullying; the other third (1/RR) would have occurred at the background rate.

Keep this apart from the population attributable fraction, which also depends on how common the exposure is in the population; the exam asks the two in consecutive items and swaps the denominators.

Rule: Attributable fraction among the exposed = (risk exposed minus risk unexposed) / risk exposed = (RR minus 1) / RR.
Trap: Reporting the attributable risk (a difference in risks) when a fraction of the exposed group's risk is asked for.
15 depressed per 100 bullied against 5 per 100 not bullied: 10 of the 15 cases among the bullied are the excess, so the attributable fraction among the exposed is 10/15 = 0.67.

Source: Last JM (2001). A Dictionary of Epidemiology, 4th ed. Oxford University Press.

Challenge 21 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.25
Heterogeneity statisticReported valueConventional reading
Chi-square (Cochran's Q) test p value0.02Below 0.10: heterogeneity detected
I squared65%Between 50% (moderate) and 75% (high): substantial
Heterogeneity statistics reported by the meta-analysis
A meta-analysis reports a chi-square test for heterogeneity with p = 0.02 and I squared of 65%, as shown in the table. The best interpretation is
  1. The pooled effect is significant
  2. The trials are homogeneous
  3. There is substantial heterogeneity and a random-effects model should be considered
  4. Publication bias is present
  5. The fixed-effect model is preferable
Show the working
Answer: C There is substantial heterogeneity and a random-effects model should be considered

Cochran's Q tests whether the studies differ more than chance allows; it has low power, so p < 0.10 is often used. I squared converts Q into the percentage of variation due to heterogeneity: roughly 25% low, 50% moderate, 75% high.

Rule: Heterogeneity: Q test p < 0.10 or I squared over 50% = substantial.
Trap: Reading the heterogeneity p value as the significance of the treatment effect.
I squared 65%: about two thirds of the variation between the trial results is more than chance alone would produce

Source: Higgins JPT et al. (2003). Measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses. BMJ, 327: 557-560.

Challenge 22 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.8
Distribution of a serum marker in affected and unaffected people, with five candidate cut-offs
A cheap blood test is proposed for a rapidly fatal metabolic encephalopathy that can be fully reversed if treated early. The figure shows the distribution of the serum marker in affected and unaffected people; higher values indicate disease. Five candidate cut-offs are marked. Which cut-off is most appropriate for a screening programme in this situation?
  1. A
  2. B
  3. C
  4. D
  5. E
Show the working
Answer: A A

Two overlapping distributions cannot be separated cleanly. Every cut-off trades false negatives against false positives. Which way to lean depends on the cost of each error: if missing a case is catastrophic and a false positive just leads to a confirmatory test, lean towards sensitivity.

With higher values indicating disease, the lowest cut-off (A at 45 units) places almost all of the affected distribution above the line, so hardly anyone with the disease is missed. It also labels a good share of the unaffected as positive, which is acceptable because they can be cleared by a second test and because the alternative is an untreated fatal illness.

The exam reverses this with a disease that is untreatable or where a positive label is itself harmful, in which case you lean towards specificity. Always read which side of the figure is 'positive' before choosing.

Rule: Fatal and treatable: choose the cut-off that minimises false negatives, accepting more false positives.
Trap: Choosing the cut-off where the two curves cross because it looks 'balanced'.
Cut-offMarker valueSensitivitySpecificityCases missed
A4599.4%73.4%0.6%
B5296.4%93.3%3.6%
C6084.1%99.4%15.9%
D6857.9%100.0%42.1%
E7627.4%100.0%72.6%
Computed from the two normal curves in the figure (unaffected mean 40, SD 8; affected mean 70, SD 10): cut-off A misses only 0.6% of cases, the fewest, which is what a fatal but curable disease demands.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Challenge 23 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.8
Receiver operating characteristic curve of a seven-item self-rated anxiety scale against a structured interview in 310 primary care attenders, with the diagonal reference line; numbered cut-offs
A seven-item self-rated anxiety scale was evaluated against a structured diagnostic interview in 310 primary care attenders, and the figure was plotted from the data. What does the dotted diagonal line on the graph represent?
  1. The curve of a scale that does not discriminate anxious from non-anxious people
  2. The curve of the structured interview used as the reference standard
  3. The curve of the scale that best discriminates anxious from non-anxious people
  4. The median survival line
  5. The curve of a scale that discriminates partially
Show the working
Answer: A The curve of a scale that does not discriminate anxious from non-anxious people

The diagonal from (0,0) to (1,1) is where sensitivity equals 1 minus specificity. A test on that line flags the same proportion of cases and non-cases at every threshold, so it carries no information about who has the disorder.

The anxiety scale's curve sits well above the diagonal, showing that at each cut-off it finds more cases than it falsely flags. The further the curve from the diagonal, the larger the AUC and the better the discrimination.

The exam asks about the diagonal, the top-left corner (perfect test) and the elbow (best balance). Know what each landmark means.

Rule: The ROC diagonal is the line of no discrimination.
Trap: Taking the diagonal for the reference standard or a 'baseline' good test.
LandmarkWhat it meansInterpretation
Dotted diagonalSensitivity = 1 minus specificity at every cut-offNo discriminating power, AUC 0.5 (the answer)
Top-left cornerSensitivity 1, false positive rate 0Perfect test
Elbow of the curveSensitivity plus specificity largestBest balance (cut 6 here)
Distance above the diagonalLarger area under the curveBetter discrimination
Landmarks of a ROC plot: the diagonal is the no-information line, the corner is perfection and the elbow is the balance point.

Source: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

Challenge 24 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.10
Hazard ratio for relapse on maintenance treatment versus placebo, with its 95% confidence interval
The figure shows the hazard ratio for relapse on maintenance treatment versus placebo reported by a survival analysis: 0.6 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.80). This means
  1. Patients on treatment relapse 60% less often
  2. At any moment, the instantaneous risk of relapse on treatment is 60% of that on placebo
  3. Median survival is 40% longer on treatment
  4. The result is not statistically significant
  5. Treatment prevents relapse in 40% of patients
Show the working
Answer: B At any moment, the instantaneous risk of relapse on treatment is 60% of that on placebo

The hazard is the rate at which events occur among those still at risk. A hazard ratio of 0.6 means a 40% lower rate of relapse at any given time on treatment. It assumes the ratio is constant over time (proportional hazards).

Rule: HR = ratio of instantaneous event rates; HR below 1 favours the first group; null is 1.
Trap: Reading HR 0.6 as 'relapse 60% less often'.
TermFormula or meaningThis item
HazardInstantaneous rate of relapse among those still at riskThe quantity being compared
Hazard ratio 0.6Rate on treatment is 60% of the rate on placebo at any moment: 40% lowerCorrect
Relapse 60% less oftenWould be HR 0.4Wrong number
Median survival 40% longerHR does not convert directly to mediansNot implied
Interval 0.45 to 0.80Excludes 1Statistically significant
A hazard ratio compares event rates at every moment of follow-up; 0.6 means 40% lower, and the interval excluding 1 makes it significant.

Source: Spruance SL et al. (2004). Hazard ratio in clinical trials. Antimicrob Agents Chemother, 48: 2787-2792.

Challenge 25 · 13.5 Inference, errors, power and confidence intervals · 3.2.17
95% confidence interval for the mean intramuscular haloperidol dose: 7.5 mg to 12.5 mg
The figure shows the 95% confidence limits for the mean intramuscular haloperidol dose used in rapid tranquillisation: 7.5 mg and 12.5 mg. Which could be the 90% confidence limits?
  1. 6 and 11 mg
  2. 7.9 and 12.1 mg
  3. 9 and 15 mg
  4. 7.5 and 12.5 mg
  5. 9 and 12.5 mg
Show the working
Answer: B 7.9 and 12.1 mg

Both intervals are centred on the sample mean (here 10 mg). The 90% interval uses a smaller multiplier, so its limits lie inside those of the 95% interval. Any option that is wider, shifted or asymmetric cannot be right.

Rule: The 90% CI sits inside the 95% CI, centred on the same estimate.
Trap: Picking an interval that is narrower but not centred on the same mean.
Same centre, shorter arms: the 90% interval sits inside the 95% interval around the same mean of 10 mg

Source: Gardner MJ, Altman DG (1986). Confidence intervals rather than P values. BMJ, 292: 746-750.

Challenge 26 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.8
A 12-item psychological distress questionnaire against a diagnostic interview in 600 primary care attenders; each labelled point is a cut-off score
A 12-item psychological distress questionnaire is compared against a diagnostic interview in 600 primary care attenders. Each labelled point on the plot corresponds to a different cut-off score for a positive screen. What is this type of plot called?
  1. A funnel plot
  2. A receiver operating characteristic curve
  3. A Galbraith plot
  4. A L'Abbe plot
  5. A scatter plot with a fitted line
Show the working
Answer: B A receiver operating characteristic curve

A receiver operating characteristic curve summarises a continuous or ordinal test across every possible threshold. For each cut-off you calculate sensitivity (true positive rate) and 1 minus specificity (false positive rate) and plot one against the other. Joining the points gives the curve. The diagonal from bottom-left to top-right represents a useless test; the closer the curve hugs the top-left corner, the better the test. The area under the curve summarises overall discrimination.

In this plot the labelled points are cut-off scores on the questionnaire. Moving from cut 11 to cut 7 the sensitivity rises (more cases caught) while the false positive rate also rises (more well people flagged), tracing the usual trade-off. The area of 0.88 indicates good discrimination.

The exam tests recognition by naming several plots used in meta-analysis as distractors. Axes labelled sensitivity and 1 minus specificity, or true and false positive rates, mean ROC every time.

Rule: Sensitivity on the y axis, 1 minus specificity on the x axis, one point per cut-off = ROC curve.
Trap: Confusing the ROC curve with meta-analysis graphics because all are 'plots used in appraisal'.
TermFormula or meaningThis item
ROC curveSensitivity against 1 minus specificity, one point per cut-offThe plot shown: labelled cut-offs 7 to 11, area 0.88
Funnel plotEffect size against precision, one point per trialMeta-analysis, not diagnosis
Galbraith plotz statistic against precision, one point per trialMeta-analysis heterogeneity
L'Abbe plotExperimental against control event rate, one point per trialMeta-analysis
Scatter with fitted lineTwo continuous variables, one point per subjectPoints here are cut-offs, not people
Axes of sensitivity and 1 minus specificity, with points that are cut-off scores, name the plot a ROC curve

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Challenge 27 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.10
Time to first relapse after a first episode of psychosis: 300 patients randomised to an early intervention service or standard care
The Kaplan-Meier plot shows time to first relapse in 300 patients with first-episode psychosis randomised to an early intervention service or standard community care, followed for 36 months. The note on the figure gives a hazard ratio of 0.56 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.77) with a log-rank p = 0.001. Which statement is the best interpretation?
  1. At 36 months, 56% of early intervention patients had relapsed compared with standard care
  2. The risk of relapse in the early intervention arm was 56% lower at every time point
  3. At any given moment, the instantaneous rate of relapse in the early intervention arm was about 44% lower than in standard care, and this difference is unlikely to be due to chance
  4. The median time to relapse was 0.56 times shorter with early intervention
  5. The two curves differ by 0.56 in proportion relapse free at the end of follow-up
Show the working
Answer: C At any given moment, the instantaneous rate of relapse in the early intervention arm was about 44% lower than in standard care, and this difference is unlikely to be due to chance

A hazard is the instantaneous rate of the event among those still at risk. The hazard ratio compares that rate between arms, averaged over the whole follow-up under the assumption that it stays constant over time (proportional hazards). It is not a risk at a fixed time, and it is not a ratio of medians, though with proportional hazards a lower HR does go with a longer median.

HR 0.56 means the relapse rate in the early intervention arm, at any moment, was 0.56 of the rate in standard care: 1 minus 0.56 = 44% lower. The 95% CI 0.41 to 0.77 lies wholly below 1, agreeing with the log-rank p = 0.001, so the difference is statistically significant. The curves are consistent with this: the early intervention curve stays above the standard care curve throughout.

The exam often swaps the reduction and the ratio (0.56 versus 44%) or presents the HR as if it were a risk difference. Say the sentence to yourself: 'the rate was 0.56 times as high'. The log-rank test and the Cox HR answer related but different questions: one tests whether the curves differ, the other says by how much.

Rule: HR = ratio of instantaneous event rates; HR 0.56 = 44% lower hazard.
Trap: Reading 0.56 as a 56% reduction.
The hazard ratio 0.56 and its whole interval 0.41 to 0.77 lie below 1: a 44% lower relapse rate at any moment, p = 0.001.

Source: Bland JM, Altman DG (2004). The logrank test. BMJ, 328: 1073.

Challenge 28 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.25
Galbraith plot: each study's standardised effect against its precision, with the fitted line and its plus or minus 2 band; one study lies outside the band
The figure shows a Galbraith plot. What does a study lying outside the two parallel lines indicate?
  1. Publication bias
  2. That study is an outlier contributing to heterogeneity
  3. That study has the largest sample
  4. The pooled estimate is not significant
  5. The study should be given more weight
Show the working
Answer: B That study is an outlier contributing to heterogeneity

Each study's effect divided by its standard error is plotted against 1 over its standard error. In a homogeneous set about 95% of points fall within the band; those outside merit a look at design, population or quality.

Rule: Galbraith plot: z score against precision; outside the band = heterogeneity.
Trap: Confusing it with the funnel plot.

Challenge 29 · 13.3 Prevalence, incidence, survival and mortality · 3.2.11
QuantityNumber
People with bipolar disorder followed for one year2,400
Deaths from cardiovascular disease during the year48
One-year follow-up of a cohort with bipolar disorder
Over one year, 48 of a cohort of 2,400 people with bipolar disorder die from cardiovascular disease. The table shows the two counts. Which measure does the figure 48/2,400 represent?
  1. Case fatality rate
  2. Crude mortality rate
  3. Cause-specific mortality rate
  4. Proportional mortality rate
  5. Standardised mortality ratio
Show the working
Answer: C Cause-specific mortality rate

Four mortality measures use similar numbers in different places. Crude mortality is all deaths over population. Cause-specific mortality is deaths from one cause over population. Proportional mortality is deaths from one cause over all deaths. Case fatality is deaths from a disease over people with that disease.

Here the numerator is cardiovascular deaths (one cause) and the denominator is the whole cohort with bipolar disorder (the population at risk), so this is the cardiovascular-specific mortality rate in that cohort, 20 per 1,000 per year. The people did not die of bipolar disorder, so it is not a case fatality rate for bipolar disorder.

The exam swaps the denominator to make a different measure; always check whether it is the population, all deaths, or the diseased.

Rule: Cause-specific mortality = deaths from that cause / population at risk; proportional mortality = deaths from that cause / all deaths.
Trap: Calling it case fatality because the cohort all have a diagnosis.
StepWorkingResult
1Numerator: deaths from one cause (cardiovascular)48
2Denominator: the population at risk (the cohort)2,400
348 / 2,4000.02 = 20 per 1,000 per year
4Name: one cause over the populationCause-specific mortality rate
Cardiovascular deaths over the whole cohort, 48/2,400, is 20 per 1,000 per year, a cause-specific mortality rate.

Source: Last JM (2001). A Dictionary of Epidemiology, 4th ed. Oxford University Press.

Challenge 30 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.8
ROC curves for two bedside delirium screening tools against a reference psychiatric assessment in 420 older medical inpatients
The ROC curves compare two bedside delirium screening tools, the Ward Confusion Screen (WCS) and the Brief Attention Test (BAT), against a reference psychiatric assessment in 420 older medical inpatients. Labelled points show the sensitivity and false positive rate at each cut-off score. The area under the WCS curve is 0.90. What does this value mean?
  1. 90% of patients screened with the WCS are correctly classified
  2. The WCS has a sensitivity of 90% at its best cut-off
  3. If one patient with delirium and one without are chosen at random, there is a 90% probability that the patient with delirium has the higher WCS score
  4. 90% of positive WCS results are true positives
  5. The WCS detects 90% of delirium when the prevalence is 50%
Show the working
Answer: C If one patient with delirium and one without are chosen at random, there is a 90% probability that the patient with delirium has the higher WCS score

The area under a ROC curve has a precise interpretation: take one person with the condition and one without, at random; the AUC is the probability that the test ranks them correctly, that is, gives the affected person the more abnormal score. It is a cut-off-free, prevalence-free measure of how well the test separates the two groups, which is exactly why it is used to compare tests on different scales.

An AUC of 0.90 means that in 90% of such random pairs the delirious patient scores higher on the WCS. The BAT, at 0.76, would rank 76% of pairs correctly. Neither number is a sensitivity, specificity or predictive value, and neither tells you which cut-off to use in practice.

The exam offers 'percentage correctly classified' and 'sensitivity of 90%' as plausible-sounding distractors. The ranking-of-pairs definition is the one to hold onto; it is also equal to the Mann-Whitney U statistic divided by the product of the two group sizes.

Rule: AUC = probability that a random case outscores a random non-case; 0.5 chance, 1.0 perfect.
Trap: Reading the AUC as accuracy or as sensitivity.
AUC 0.90: in 90 of 100 random case and non-case pairs the WCS ranks the delirious patient higher; the BAT (0.76) would manage 76.

Source: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

C) A test with no discriminating ability, where sensitivity equals the false positive rate at every cut-off (AUC 0.5)

Remember. The diagonal is the chance line: sensitivity = 1 minus specificity, AUC 0.5. (Diagonal = coin toss = AUC 0.5)

Trap. Mistaking the chance line for the line of equal sensitivity and specificity.

Why not the others.
A) The best possible test: The best possible test hugs the left and top edges, as far from the diagonal as possible.
B) The point of optimal cut-off for each test: Optimal cut-offs are points on the curves, usually the point nearest the top left corner.

Which conclusion is supported by inspection of the figure?

Remember. Compare subgroups with the test for subgroup differences; a non-significant test means no evidence of difference, not proof of sameness. (Overlapping subtotal diamonds and p = 0.90 = no evidence tiers differ)

Trap. Choosing 'the studies are homogeneous', which claims proof of a null.

Why not the others.
A) The individual studies are homogeneous in their effect sizes: Homogeneity can never be proved; a non-significant test only fails to detect heterogeneity, and the exam will not accept a claim of homogeneity.
B) There is significant heterogeneity in effect size within every tier: Every subtotal shows p of 0.64 or higher with I squared 0%; none shows significant heterogeneity.
